October 2nd, 2026 | 2:46pm EST

County Council Meeting 09.17.2026
Election Results

The regular meeting of the Northampton County Council was held on the above date with the following present: Jeff Warren, Vice President; Jason B. Boulette; Theresa Fadem; David Holland; Kelly Keegan; Lori Vargo Heffner; Nadeem Qayyum; Alene M. Shafnisky, Clerk to Council; Courtney Christman, Executive Secretary to Council; and Matthew J. Deschler, Solicitor to Council. Absent were Kenneth M. Kraft and Thomas A. Giovanni.



Pledge of Allegiance 


Mr. Holland led the pledge of allegiance.



Moment of Silence/Prayer 


Mr. Warren held a moment of silence.



Approval of the Minutes – September 3, 2026 


Ms. Keegan made the following motion:


Be It Moved By the Northampton County Council that the minutes of the September 3, 2026 meeting shall be approved.  


Ms. Fadem seconded the motion.


The minutes were approved by voice acclamation. 


Courtesy of the Floor


Mr. Joe Welsh, East Allen Township, PA – stated that he fully supported Ms. Dawn Godshall with her lengthy history and experience to serve with the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission.



County Executive Report


Ms. Tara Zrinski, County Executive, stated that she wished to acknowledge all who were lost on September 11, 2001, as well as those emergency service and first responders who answer when people are their most in need. She further stated she had spoken on Patriots Day and presented the Patriot Day Valor Award to Todd Weaver in recognition of his 29 years of service to Northampton County.


Ms. Zrinski advised that she and the new Director of Continuum of Care at Gracedale visited Phoebe Nursing Home, and brought many ideas back that could be useful at Gracedale. She further advised that they were doing what they could to improve resident care, workforce stability, and the environment at the Home. She advised members of her Cabinet had also participated in the United Way Day of Caring cleaning headstones at Historic Easton Cemetery. 


Ms. Zrinski stated that she gave remarks at the Eastern PA Greenways and Trails Summit, focused on the relationship between economic development, transportation, quality of life and trail networks connecting communities through Northampton County. She further stated that she had toured a data center to better understand the infrastructure demands of energy, land and water use.


Ms. Zrinski advised that she wanted to address the Grand Jury 

Report focused on Gracedale, and that it had renewed public scrutiny on Gracedale for events that occurred in 2025. She further advised they had looked at these events with a great degree of scrutiny and reassured that the nurse responsible was an agency nurse who had been barred from Gracedale and faced criminal charges. She advised they were learning from past issues and moving forward with measurable action, including the grade change for Nursing Supervisors. She advised the operational plan focused on staffing, supervision, accountability, workforce stability, and resident safety. 


Ms. Zrinski stated that the Department of Economic Development hosted the Council of Governments meeting, which focused on karst geology, as well as had a meeting with a regional plan update to increase regional coordination of fire services. She further stated the Public Safety Grant Review Committee had 50 applications this year, and that the Digital Navigator Coalition would hold a training event at the YMCA on September 22nd.


Ms. Zrinski advised there were more locations for secure ballot and drop box access for the upcoming election. She further advised that they would begin the replacement of the parking deck at the beginning of October. She advised Human Services continued to provide its vital services on behavioral health, substance use recovery and public education, including participating in World Suicide Prevention Day, and were starting an awareness campaign involving purple ducks attached to cards informing people where they could reach out to, to get help. 


Ms. Zrinski stated that they also distributed Narcan resources and hosted a Live Well, Be Well event at Paxinosa Elementary School, and the Sheriff’s Department had a successful fire drill that evacuated the building in under 7 minutes. She further stated that that Sheriff’s Department had 3 deputies that completed a crisis intervention train-the-trainer session. She stated that Public Works was preparing for the Household Hazardous Waste Collection event, free for Northampton County residents.


Ms. Zrinski advised that the Department of Corrections, they brought in nationally recognized corrections experts, including a suicide prevention expert to assess the Prison and develop proactive practices within the next 6 to 8 weeks. She further advised that the Public Defender’s Office had developed a QR code to easily apply for representation. 


In response to Ms. Vargo Heffner’s question, Ms. Zrinski stated that the litigation about the ballots had just been decided that day so they could not yet announce a firm date to begin voting-on-demand.


In response to Mr. Qayyum’s question, Ms. Zrinski stated the goal of agency nurses was to go under 20% agency nurses by reducing the census and hiring more people. She further advised that because of the inflated cost of agency nurses, even with high raises Gracedale would remain under the amount they were paying the agencies.


In response to Mr. Holland’s question about why she tried to quash the Grand Jury Report, Ms. Zrinski, Mr. Aurand and Ms. Rudas advised that the Report was based on one sided testimony, and did not have anything constructive to offer the public, and was very inflammatory as a result. Ms. Zrinski also alleged that perjury was also included in the Report, and it offered no positive suggestions or fact checked testimony.

Effective Date:


In accordance with Northampton County Home Rule Charter Section 705(e) this ordinance shall become effective upon the date of enactment.



Mr. Warren stated the public hearing, discussion and possible vote on this ordinance would take place on October 1, 2026.



Consideration of the Executive’s Appointments Resolution: Drug and Alcohol Advisory Board; Lehigh Valley Planning Commission


Mr. Holland introduced the following resolution:


R.96-2026. RESOLVED, by the Northampton County Council that the following individuals shall be confirmed in their appointments as indicated hereafter:



Drug and Alcohol Advisory Board

Appointment:

Donna Thorman   Term to Expire: 06/30/28

93 Seyfried Ave

Nazareth, PA 18064



Lehigh Valley Planning Commission 

Appointments:    Terms to Expire: 12/31/29

Dawn Godshall

231 Tomahawk Trail 

Northampton PA, 18067


Robert Melosky

475 Pine Top Trail

Bethlehem PA, 18017



Ms. Vargo Heffner indicated she had served with Ms. Thorman on the Mental Health Advisory Board and highly supported her appointment. Mr. Boulette shared that Ms. Godshall and Mr. Melosky had introduced themselves at the Personnel Committee meeting and appeared to be very good candidates.



As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Boulette, “yes” and Fadem, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



Consideration of Personnel Request Resolutions: 

a) Fiscal Affairs


Mr. Holland introduced the following resolution:


R.97-2026. IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED, by the Northampton County Council that the position of one (1) full-time Communications Manager, pay grade CS/GR31/1-A, salary $79,431 (total salary and benefits $114,021), in the Department of Fiscal Affairs, shall be downgraded to pay grade CS/GR23/1-A, salary $54,962 (total salary and benefits $87,655), effective September 18, 2026.

  


As there were no comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Boulette, “yes” and Fadem, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



b. Gracedale 


Mr. Holland introduced the following resolution:


R.98-2026. IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council that eight (8) full-time Nursing Supervisors, pay grade CS/GR29/1-A, salary $579,552 (total salary and benefits $897,325), shall be upgraded to pay grade CS/GR32, with a salary commensurate with experience, qualifications and/or education at the discretion of the Director of Continuum of Care for Gracedale to fall between Step 1-A, salary $665,376 (total salary and benefits $994,512) and Step 7-G, salary $866,488 (total salary and benefits $1,222,251), in Gracedale Nursing Home, effective September 18, 2026.  


IT IS FURTHER RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council that one (1) full-time Nursing Supervisor, pay grade CS/GR29/5-E, salary $86,391 (total salary and benefits $127,959), shall be upgraded to pay grade CS/GR32, with a salary commensurate with experience, qualifications and/or education at the discretion of the Director of Continuum of Care for Gracedale to fall between Step 3-C, salary $90,826 (total salary and benefits $132,981) and Step 7-G, salary $108,311 (total salary and benefits $152,782), in Gracedale Nursing Home effective September 18, 2026.  


IT IS FURTHER RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council that seven (7) part-time Nursing Supervisors, pay grade CS/GR29/1-A, salary $202,843 (total salary and benefits $229,699), shall be upgraded to pay grade CS/GR32, with a salary commensurate with experience, qualifications and/or education at the discretion of the Director of Continuum of Care for Gracedale to fall between Step 1-A, salary $232,881 (total salary and benefits $263,714) and Step 7-G, salary $303,270 (total salary and benefits $343,423), in Gracedale Nursing Home effective September 18, 2026. 


IT IS FURTHER RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council that one (1) part-time Nursing Supervisor, pay grade CS/GR29/5-E, salary $34,556 (total salary and benefits $46,632), shall be upgraded to pay grade CS/GR32, with a salary commensurate with experience, qualifications and/or education at the discretion of the Director of Continuum of Care for Gracedale to fall between Step 3-C, salary $36,330 (total salary and benefits $48,640) and Step 7-G, salary $43,234 (total salary and benefits $56,560), in Gracedale Nursing Home effective September 18, 2026.  


IT IS FURTHER RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council that nine (9) per diem Nursing Supervisors, pay grade CS/GR29A/1-A, salary $108,576 (total salary and benefits $122,951), shall be upgraded to pay grade CS/GR32, with a salary commensurate with experience, qualifications and/or education at the discretion of the Director of Continuum of Care for Gracedale to fall between Step 1-A, salary $149,709 (total salary and benefits $169,531) and Step 7-G, salary $194,959 (total salary and benefits $220,771), in Gracedale Nursing Home effective September 18, 2026.  



In response to Ms. Vargo Heffner’s question, Mr. Michael Colon, Deputy Director of Human Resources, stated that rather than move to the highest possible pay grade, which would create pay compression at the top levels of Gracedale Administration, the Department had asked for the ability to place new Supervisors on Grade 32, at a step anywhere from 1-A to 7-G. He stated this was for vacant positions, and that the existing Nursing Supervisors would also be upgraded.


In response to Mr. Holland’s question, Mr. Colon advised that this was merely the first step, and the union negotiation would be next.


Ms. Zrinski stated that Grade 38 would put Nursing Supervisors on the same level as the Nursing Home Administrator, and by using the newly proposed scale they would still reach their target pay level without creating compression. In response to Ms. Fadem’s question, Ms. Zrinski stated that employees did not necessarily get a step every year they had a positive review; it depended on the view of the County Executive in office to determine if steps or COLAs were granted or not. She further stated that at Gracedale, they had to have performance evaluations of every employee, every year.



As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Boulette, “yes” and Fadem “yes.”

The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



Consideration of a Resolution Approving the Application for and Acceptance of Funds Through the Local Share Account on Behalf of Historic Bethlehem Museum & Sites, Inc.


Mr. Boulette introduced the following resolution:


R.99-2026. A RESOLUTION APPROVING THE APPLICATION FOR AND ACCEPTANCE OF FUNDS THROUGH THE LOCAL SHARE ACCOUNT ON BEHALF OF HISTORIC BETHLEHEM MUSEUMS AND SITES, INC.



WHEREAS, The PA Race Horse Development and Gaming Act (Act 2004-71), as amended, has established the Pennsylvania Gaming Local Share Account (Local Share Account) under the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA) for the purpose of distributing 2% of gross terminal revenues of certain licensed gaming facilities in an orderly and timely fashion to support and enhance community and economic well-being and mitigate the impact of gaming and related activities; and


WHEREAS, the Northampton County Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) and Historic Bethlehem Museums and Sites, Inc. (HBMS) have prepared all the documentation necessary to submit a request for this funding. 

 

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by Northampton County Council that the County of Northampton does hereby request a Monroe County Local Share Assessment grant in the amount of $454,415 as a pass-through entity on behalf of HBMS from the CFA to fund the next phase of the 1761 Tannery restoration, part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Moravian Church Settlements – Bethlehem, anticipated to cover vat room improvements – including a new sump structure, pump, and stone infill – along with associated plumbing, electrical, and lighting work.

 

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED by Northampton County Council that the County of Northampton does hereby request a Northampton & Lehigh Counties Local Share Assessment grant in the amount of $454,415 as a pass-through entity on behalf of HBMS from the CFA to fund the next phase of the 1761 Tannery restoration, part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Moravian Church Settlements – Bethlehem, anticipated to cover vat room improvements – including a new sump structure, pump, and stone infill – along with associated plumbing, electrical, and lighting work.


BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Council of Northampton County Council does hereby designate the County Executive to execute all documents and agreements between the County of Northampton and the CFA to facilitate and assist in obtaining the requested grant and that the Director of Northampton County DCED is designated as the second signatory on all documents and agreements.



Mr. Warren noted the next 2 LSA Account requests came in after the Economic Development Committee, but were time sensitive and had to be considered tonight. He offered anyone present to comment on the resolution under consideration.


Ms. Lindsay Jancay, Vice President and Managing Director of Historic Bethlehem Museum and Sites, stating that this funding would allow them to address the Tannery’s bathroom with a new pump and infill so that it could continue to expand as it was the last building of its kind that still existed on Earth, and they had hoped to bring in 500 students who had never experienced the Colonial Industrial Quarter.


Mr. Holland advised that the public should know this was funded as part of the gross terminal revenues from the PA Resource Development Gaming Act, rather than being County funds or tax dollars.



As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Boulette, “yes”; Qayyum, “abstain”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Holland, “yes” and Keegan, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 6-0-1 abstention.



Consideration of a Resolution Approving the Application for and Acceptance of Funds Through the Local Share Account on Behalf of Suburban Medical Services


Mr. Boulette introduced the following resolution:


R.100-2026. A RESOLUTION APPROVING THE APPLICATION FOR AND ACCEPTANCE OF FUNDS THROUGH THE LOCAL SHARE ACCOUNT ON BEHALF OF SUBURBAN EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES


WHEREAS, The PA Race Horse Development and Gaming Act (Act 2004-71), as amended, has established the Pennsylvania Gaming Local Share Account (Local Share Account) under the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA) for the purpose of distributing 2% of gross terminal revenues of certain licensed gaming facilities in an orderly and timely fashion to support and enhance community and economic well-being and mitigate the impact of gaming and related activities; and


WHEREAS, the Northampton County Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) and Suburban Emergency Medical Services have prepared all the documentation necessary to submit a request for this funding. 


NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by Northampton County Council that the County of Northampton does hereby request a Northampton & Lehigh Counties Local Share Assessment grant in the amount of $271,387.00 as a pass-through entity on behalf of Suburban Emergency Medical Services for a 2027 Ford E350 Crestline CCL150 Ambulance.


BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Northampton County Council does hereby designate the County Executive to execute all documents and agreements between the County of Northampton and the CFA to facilitate and assist in obtaining the requested grant, and that the Director of Northampton County DCED is designated as the second signatory on all documents and agreements.



Mr. Jeff Young, Grant Coordinator at Suburban Medical Services, stated that EMS services struggled across the State and country, and they were trying to upgrade their fleet. He further stated that that they began in 1953 serving Wilson, West Easton and Palmer, and now worked with 14 Northampton County communities and 5 in Monroe County. He said they were a mostly paid service, because there were so few volunteers to run shifts regularly.


As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Boulette, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Holland, “yes” and Keegan, “yes.”

The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



Consideration of Livable Landscapes Grant Award Resolutions:

a) Trail Corridor Acquisition in City of Easton


Ms. Keegan introduced the following resolution:

R.101-2026. WHEREAS, the County of Northampton implemented the Northampton County Open Space Initiative enacting the Northampton County Open Space Ordinance #423-2004 on November 5, 2004; and


WHEREAS, the County of Northampton implemented the Livable Landscapes Open Space Plan Program and further provided for the administration of the 21st Century Open Space Initiative, enacted as the Northampton County Livable Landscapes Ordinance #603-2015 on January 7, 2016; and


WHEREAS, the County of Northampton implemented the Livable Landscapes Grant Program Guidelines to replace the Environmental Services Assistance Grant Guidelines, enacting the adoption of the Livable Landscapes Grant Program Guidelines Ordinance #673-2019 on July 18, 2019; and 


WHEREAS, under the Livable Landscapes Grant Program, Northampton County authorized funding to be allocated for land preservation, ecological restoration, planning, education and outreach, and municipal park acquisition, development, and rehabilitation in order to assist organizations and Northampton County municipalities to acquire, restore, and enhance permanently protected lands to conserve natural resources and provide outdoor recreation for future generations; and


WHEREAS, the City of Easton, a Third-Class City that operates as a Home Rule municipality, has worked with the County on regional trail projects under the Lehigh Valley Trail Connection Strategy, Northampton County Livable Landscapes Plan, and Two Rivers Trail Plan; and 


WHEREAS, the City of Easton has been awarded grant funding from the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources and the PA Department of Transportation for the acquisition of five (5) inactive rail parcels and an inactive trestle bridge (“The Highline”), a major trail gap initiative; and  


WHEREAS, the acquisition will lead to a major trail gap being acquired for the September 11th National Memorial Trail, Two Rivers Trail and as an alternative to the D&L Trail; and


WHEREAS, Northampton County through its Livable Landscapes Program has assisted with funding in the acquisition of major trail gaps throughout the County.


  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Northampton County Council:


1. Authorizes the Northampton County Executive, through the Division of Parks, Recreation & Conservation, or their designee, to take any and all steps necessary to administer and complete Northampton County’s obligations.


2. Approves the funding for all related acquisition costs of the inactive rail parcels and bridge along the September 11th National Memorial Trail, co-aligned with the Two Rivers Trail within the City of Easton, not to exceed $150,000.


3. Authorizes the use of Act 13 - Marcellus Shale Legacy Funding for any and all necessary steps to finalize the acquisition of the Highline project.



As there were no comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Keegan, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Boulette, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Holland, “yes” and Qayyum, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



b) D&L Historic & Cultural Education Contractual Services


Mr. Warren advised this resolution was being withdrawn from the agenda.



Consideration of a Resolution Approving the Renaming of Fry’s Run Park to Mineo Conservation Area


Ms. Keegan introduced the following resolution:


R.102-2026. WHEREAS, Isidore “Bill” Mineo, Northampton County’s former Park Board Executive Director and Superintendent and Lorraine Mineo, a former professor at Lafayette College, were pioneers, long-time advocates and essential to the conservation, recreation and preservation of Northampton County’s landscapes; and


WHEREAS, Bill served as the first and only Executive Director of the Northampton County Park Board in 1974, until Northampton County was reorganized under Home Rule Charter, when the Park Board was dissolved and became a Division under the Department of Public Works, at which time Bill became Superintendent; and


WHEREAS, under Bill’s supervision the first major park milestone was established. Minsi Lake, owned by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and leased to Northampton County, was the first park to be operated by the County in 1975, until Fry’s Run Park was the first Northampton County owned park to be developed and opened to the public in our parks system in September 1977; and


WHEREAS, Bill worked with the Commonwealth to establish the Delaware River Scenic Drive, a number of roadside parks and overlooks, such as Wy-Hit-Tuk, Frost Hollow, Doe Hollow and Fry’s Run along PA Route 611 from Bucks County into Upper Mount Bethel Township; and


WHEREAS, Fry’s Run Park, was named for Fry’s Run, a high-quality cold-water trout stream that runs through the park on its way to the Delaware River several hundred feet downstream; and


WHEREAS, Bill and Lorraine were instrumental in collaborating with other recreation and conservation organizations to help establish the Lehigh Valley Conservancy, now known as Wildlands Conservancy, the D&L National Heritage Corridor, Northampton County Open Space Advisory Board, Williams Township Land Preservation Board, and Fry’s Run Watershed Organization; and


WHEREAS, Bill and Lorraine Mineo provided a lifetime of dedication and devotion to land conservation, ecological restoration, natural and cultural resource preservation, and greenway and watershed protection. Their passion for public lands and waterways was to enhance wildlife, water quality and native habitat, and to provide education and recreation for people of all ages and future generations, making them deserving of recognition; and


WHEREAS, Northampton County Council authorizes the renaming of Fry’s Run Park situated in Williams Township, Northampton County, Pennsylvania, to be known from this time forward as the Mineo Conservation Area. 

   

NOW, THEREFORE, IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED by Northampton County Council that:


1. The Northampton County Executive, through the Division of Parks, Recreation & Conservation, or their designee, is authorized to take any and all steps necessary to facilitate the name change.


2. Fry’s Run Park, situated within Williams Township, Northampton County, Pennsylvania, will be renamed Mineo Conservation Area and the County of Northampton to provide any and all resources to effectuate this name change, including but not limited to, the appropriate signage.



Ms. Vargo Heffner stated it was a long time coming and there were no more deserving people of this than the Mineos.


Mr. Boulette advised that the reasons they were interested in this particular park was because the Mineo family farm was in Williams Township, and had trails running from their farm to Fry’s Run Park.


As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Keegan, “yes”; Boulette, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes” and Warren, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



Consideration of a Resolution Accepting Ongoing Human Services – Mental Health Donations to the Northampton County Suicide Prevention Task Force


R.103-2026. WHEREAS, Northampton County Home Rule Charter Section 202(10) provides that County Council shall have, among others, the following powers: “to accept on behalf of the County any gifts of real property and to provide for the acceptance by any agency on behalf of the County of other gifts;” and 


WHEREAS, on September 4, 2026, the Department of Human Services - Mental Health Division requested they be allowed to accept monetary donations for the Northampton County Suicide Prevention Task Force, pursuant to a request from a family who lost a loved one and would like funds to be donated in lieu of flowers.


NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Northampton County Council authorizes the Department of Human Services – Mental Health Division to accept all monetary donations for the above-mentioned cause, to the Northampton County Suicide Prevention Task Force. 



As there were no comments or questions, Mr. Warren called for the vote on the resolution.


The vote: Boulette, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes” and Warren, “yes.”


The resolution was adopted by a vote of 7-0.



Mr. Holland began a discussion regarding the selection of the Committee Chairs, and that unilateral decision making may not be the most well considered. He suggested that perhaps while the President selected the Committee and appointed a Chair, that appointment would be confirmed by the full Council by a majority, because as of now there was no statutory-drawn rule about this. He asked if this conversation could take place at the next Governance Committee meeting in November. Discussion was held on the suggestion and it was suggested that once a decision was made a resolution or ordinance could be drafted on this policy.


Mr. Holland advised that with regard to Gracedale, as an overall discussion focusing on public trust, they had to restore the trust of the public and he thought the best way to do that was with a third-party entity coming in to provide an assessment and give direction and validation to the changes that had begun to be implemented at the Home. He further advised that he thought having an assistant with operations and recommendations as an independent agency.


Ms. Fadem stated that she was horrified at the Grand Jury Report, and knew that at a private home jobs would have been lost, and having an unrelated, independent entity to review the facility would be a good idea.



Ms. Vargo Heffner made a motion to enter Executive Session to discuss potential litigation.

Mr. Boulette seconded the motion.


Mr. Warren called for the vote.


The vote: Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Boulette, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Warren, “yes” and Fadem “yes.”


The motion passed by a vote of 7-0.


Mr. Warren stated they entered Executive Session at 7:59 p.m. and returned at 8:06 p.m. and no action and no votes were taken.



Council Committee Reports


Ms. Keegan advised they held an Energy, Environment and Land Use Committee meeting which discussed the renaming of Fry’s Run Park to Mineo Conservation Area, as well as discussing the D&L Historic and Cultural Education contractual services.

Mr. Holland stated that the Personnel Committee met and discussed the appointments from the Executive as well as trying to move forward with salary changes to start reducing the use of agency nurses.


Mr. Boulette advised that the Finance Committee met to discuss the budget amendment.


Mr. Boulette stated that a Governance Committee meeting was held to discuss draft amendments to an ordinance related to salaries and a good discussion on the legalities involved.



Council Liaison Reports


Ms. Vargo Heffner stated she attended the CJAB and AOPC task force meetings on mental health in the criminal justice system and hoped to have some technical assistance in dealing with people who were adjudicated as suffering from mental health issues. She further stated that the CCAB health task force was examining issues of health deserts across the State and was to have assessment tools to identify needs in different areas of the State to fill in the gaps.


Mr. Boulette advised he attended the Discover Lehigh Valley Board meeting, and Northampton County’s hotel bookings continued to be strong, which then funded the Hotel Tax grants.


Mr. Boulette stated he attended a Conservation District meeting and they voted on a Memorandum of Understanding with the County that would grant them an annual subsidy of $150,000 in exchange for performing services to the County focused on their primary goals of environmental stewardship and stormwater management.


Adjournment


Ms. Vargo Heffner made a motion to adjourn the meeting.


Ms. Keegan seconded the motion. 


The motion to adjourn passed unanimously by voice acclamation.

Election Results

The County of Northampton Controller's Office received a rating of "pass" in its External Quality Control Review in accordance with the guidelines of the Association of Local Government Auditors for the period January 1, 2022, though December 31, 2024.


"Based on the results of our review, it is our opinion that the County of Northampton Controller's Office internal quality control system was adequately designed and operating effectively to provide reasonable assurance of compliance with Government Auditing Standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements for engagements during the period January 1, 2022, through December 31, 2024."


The peer review was conducted by: J. TImothy Biernes, South Florida Water Management District, Office of Inspector General, CPA, CMA, CISA, CIG, CITP, CGMA, MBA; and Burce C. Landrum, Jr. Audit Manager, Milwaukee County Office of the Comptroller, MBA.

August 21st, 2026 | 10:15am EST

County Council Meeting 08.06.2026
Election Results

The regular meeting of the Northampton County Council was held on the above date with the following present: Kenneth M. Kraft, President; Jeff Warren, Vice President; Jason B. Boulette; Theresa Fadem; Thomas A. Giovanni; David Holland; Kelly Keegan; Nadeem Qayyum; Lori Vargo Heffner; Alene M. Shafnisky, Clerk to Council; Jenesia Negron, Deputy Clerk to Council, and Matthew J. Deschler, Solicitor to Council.



Pledge of Allegiance


    Mr. Giovanni led the pledge of allegiance.



Moment of Silence/Prayer


    Mr. Kraft held a moment of silence.



Approval of the Minutes – July 16, 2026

 

    Ms. Keegan made the following motion:


    Be It Moved By the Northampton County Council that the minutes of the July 16, 2026 meeting shall be approved. 


    Mr. Giovanni seconded the motion.


    The minutes were approved by voice acclamation.



Courtesy of the Floor


    Ms. Becky Bartlett, Nazareth, PA – read and submitted a letter (Attachment #1) and stated there was a public notice by Hercules Cement Company, also doing business as Buzzi Unicem, requesting a lowering of their controls on nitrogen oxides and other organic compounds in exception to Section 184 of the Clean Air Act. She further stated that these particulates were known to cause health issues.


    Ms. Bartlett advised that the Lehigh Valley had a scientifically proven problem with particulate pollution, with some of the highest asthma rates in the nation. She requested that County Council and the Administration file a formal objection to the request of Buzzi Unicem with the PA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).


    Mr. Joe Walsh, East Allen Township, PA - thanked County Council for working to preserve our Constitution by opposing the continued killing of both US Citizens and others by ICE.    


    Ms. Jaqueline Moore, Easton, PA – stated several examples that she believed demonstrated her being targeted by Easton Vice Mayor Frank Pintabone and that the police did not help her.

    


County Executive Report


    Ms. Tara Zrinski, County Executive, advised she would look into these situations, and her office would offer opposition to the Buzzi Unicem request with the PA DEP.


    Ms. Zrinski stated that the Department of Community and Economic Development had opened the Public Safety grant program, and explained where additional information could be found. She further stated the Grow Norco grant applications were being reviewed and that Hotel Room Rental Tax applicants would be reviewed shortly. She stated they continued to manage affordable housing initiatives, planned Countywide events and administered pass through grant programs.


    Ms. Zrinski advised that the Elections Office was actively interviewing applicants for the Deputy Registrar, as well as evaluating processes to improve operations. She acknowledged the Elections Commission had to cancel a meeting due to an administrative oversight.


    Ms. Zrinski stated that they continued to work diligently on the Gracedale Strategic Plan, as well as a plan to improve safety at the Prison. She further stated that staff attended National Night Out with local law enforcement, and that they were working with agencies to train in suicide awareness to avoid future tragedies.


    Ms. Zrinski advised that in response to a recent complaint, the Department of Health had visited Gracedale and found the complaint to be unsubstantiated. She stated that there was no way to change the licensing status until more time went by, but that care for the residents continued to be recognized for their compassion even while they were struggling. She presented a certificate to Shannon Aleman, who had earned the designation of a Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement Certified Professional from the American Association of Post-Acute Care Nursing, a designation recognized by the Center for Medicaid and Medicare Services.


    Ms. Zrinski stated that along with attending local national night out festivities, the Sheriff's Department welcomed people interested in law enforcement to apply for their Department and were pleased to welcome Deputy José Melendez, a military veteran, to the Sheriff's Department. She further stated that a walk-through was conducted to evaluate continued construction at the Prison, and that Public Works had been receiving proposals to replace historic Bridge 149. She stated the Department was also working on the elevators at Gracedale using grant funding, and had intended to have an alternative contract on tonight's agenda for the parking garage replacement.


    Ms. Zrinski advised that although a contract had been approved with Mohawk, it was later determined that although they had assured that they could meet the Responsible Contractors Ordinance (RCO) standards, they could not provide those required certifications. She further advised that meant the contract had to be awarded to the second highest bidder which was Wilmer R. Schultz, Inc., who had already provided documentation proving they met the RCO requirements.


    Ms. Zrinski stated they had onboarded 23 new employees, approximately half of whom were at Gracedale. She further stated that the Warden had retired from the Northampton County Prison after 34 years of service to the County. She thanked him for his extraordinary service and wished him a happy retirement. She stated the Department of Corrections had placed 10 inmates directly into inpatient facilities saving the County $33,169.50. She further stated this was important due to the current deficit situation in the budget.


    Ms. Zrinski advised that Fiscal Affairs continued to work on the 2027 budget, and in the Criminal Division they continued to provide excellent service despite ongoing staffing shortages. She further advised the transition to a fully paperless criminal case system remained a priority and they were now scanning all criminal case documents, improving electronic access for the Courts and other offices for the public. She advised Archives continued to field increased historical record requests related to America 250.


    In response to a question from Mr. Kraft, Ms. Zrinski stated that they were pursuing available grants for anything they could find at the Prison including historical preservation money.



Consideration of a Resolution Approving the Annual Action Plan for Fiscal Year 2026 for the County of Northampton


    Mr. Warren introduced the following resolution:


R.78-2026. A resolution approving the aNNual action plan for fiscal year 2026 for the county of Northampton

 

 

WHEREAS, under Title I of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, as amended, the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) is authorized to extend financial assistance to communities in the prevention or elimination of slums or urban blight, or activities which will benefit low- and moderate-income persons, or other urgent community development needs; and

WHEREAS, under the HOME program created by the National Affordable Housing Act of 1990, as amended, the Secretary of HUD is authorized to extend financial assistance to participating jurisdictions to expand the supply of decent, safe, sanitary, and affordable housing; and

WHEREAS, under the ESG program created by the McKinney Homeless Assistance Act of 1987, Title IV, Subtitle B, as amended, the Secretary of HUD is authorized to extend financial assistance to participating jurisdictions to Engage homeless individuals and families living on the street; Improve the number and quality of emergency shelters for homeless individuals and families; Help operate these shelters; Provide essential services to shelter residents; Rapidly re-house homeless individuals and families; and Prevent families and individuals from becoming homeless; and

WHEREAS, the County under its Citizen Participation plan engaged the community, collaborated with other public and private partners that assisted in the development and review of the Annual Action Plan, towards the County’s efforts in directing HUD funding programs for the FY 2026 program year; and

 

WHEREAS, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has advised the County of Northampton that under Fiscal Year 2026, the County is eligible to apply for an entitlement grant under the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Program in the amount of $2,228,708, the HOME Investment Partnership Program (HOME) in the amount of $660,306.06, and the Emergency Solutions Grants Program (ESG) in the amount of $197,804; and

WHEREAS, the County of Northampton’s Department of Community and Economic Development has prepared a FY 2026 Annual Action Plan which proposes how the entitlement grant funds will be expended to address the housing and community development needs identified in the County’s Five-Year Consolidated Plan; and

Now, therefore, be it resolved by the Council of the County of Northampton:

 

1. That the FY 2026 Annual Action Plan, is hereby approved; and


2. That the County is fully informed of any conditions that are required in the undertaking and carrying out of housing and community development activities with Federal financial assistance; and


3. That the County Executive is authorized to execute and file the financial assistance application forms with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) which has indicated its willingness to make these funds available to carry out the CDBG Program in the amount of two million two hundred twenty eight thousand seven hundred and eight dollars ($2,228,708), HOME Program funding in the amount of six hundred sixty thousand three hundred six dollars and six cents ($660,306.06), ESG Program funding in the amount of one hundred ninety-seven thousand eight hundred and four dollars ($197,804), and is further authorized to act as the authorized representative of the County of Northampton to sign any and all documents in regard to these programs; and


4. That the County Executive is hereby authorized to provide assurances and/or certifications as required by HUD and also provide any additional documents that may be requested.

    As there were no comments or questions, Mr. Kraft called for the vote on the resolution.


    The vote: Warren, “yes”; Giovanni, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Kraft, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Boulette, “yes” and Fadem, “yes.”


    The resolution was adopted by a vote of 9-0.



Consideration of a Resolution Approving the Formal Request of a Main Street Matters Program Grant on Behalf of ArtsQuest


    Mr. Warren introduced the following resolution:


R.79-2026. A resolution approving tHE formal request OF a main street matters program grant on behalf of ARTSQUEST

 

 

WHEREAS, The Main Street Matters program (MSM), through the Department of Community and Economic Development of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, is designed to support downtown cores and surrounding neighborhoods with tools to create healthy, vibrant, and welcoming communities; and funding is available to support revitalization efforts in planning, business support, aesthetic improvements, and the increase of safety and security; and

WHEREAS, the Northampton County Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) and ArtsQuest have prepared all the documentation necessary to submit a request for this funding.

 

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED the County of Northampton hereby approves submitting a request as the eligible applicant on behalf of ArtsQuest, for a Main Street Matters Program grant in the amount of $350,000 to transform the plaza spaces adjacent to the 150-year-old Bethlehem Steel Turn & Grind Shop and the Bethlehem Visitor’s Center into a multi-purpose hub for public exhibitions and festivals, including ArtsQuest’s annual Musikfest festival and Christkindlmarkt holiday market, that will attract visitors from across the nation and around the world, boosting the local economy for hotels, restaurants, and small businesses across the Lehigh Valley.                        

be it further RESOLVED that the Council of Northampton County does hereby designate the County Executive to execute all documents and agreements to facilitate and assist in obtaining the requested grant and that the Director of Northampton County Department of Community and Economic Development is designated as the second signatory on all documents and agreements.


    

    As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Kraft called for the vote on the amended resolution.


    The vote: Warren, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Kraft, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Boulette, “yes”; Fadem, “yes” and Giovanni, “yes.”


    The resolution was adopted by a vote of 9-0.



Consideration of a Pilot Program for Farmers’ Market Access Resolution


    Mr. Boulette introduced the following resolution:


    R.80-2026. WHEREAS, farmers’ markets are vital resources for the community that increase access to fresh food, strengthen social connections, and support the local farmers that are a bedrock of the Northampton County economy; and


    WHEREAS, producer-only farmers’ markets are those where vendors sell items they have grown or made themselves, thus providing fresher goods harvested more recently and that have traveled a shorter distance; and


    WHEREAS, Northampton County has seven (7) producer-only farmers’ markets in the form of the Bethlehem Farmers’ Market, the Easton Farmers’ Market, the West Ward Market, the Farm Market at Northampton Community College, the Nazareth Farmers’ Market, the Northampton Borough Farmers’ Market, and the Saucon Valley Farmers’ Market; and


    WHEREAS, 2025 data indicates that farmers’ markets have a dedicated customer base across Pennsylvania, with 38% of shoppers visiting weekly, and with shoppers spending an average of $31.24 per visit; and


    WHEREAS, surveys conducted by Buy Fresh Buy Local-Greater Lehigh Valley (BFBL-GLV) show that in the Lehigh Valley, the share of customers spending $30 or more per visit rose from 19% in 2019 to 28.1% in 2023; and

 

    WHEREAS, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania provides funding for the Senior Farmers’ Market Nutrition Program (FMNP), administered by each county’s Area Agency on Aging, to give vouchers to seniors which can be redeemed for food from participating farmers; and


    WHEREAS, in 2023 Senior FMNP benefits were doubled from $25 across five $5 vouchers to $50 across five $10 vouchers; and


    WHEREAS, this increase in benefits increased the number of vouchers redeemed in the Lehigh Valley, from $31,000 redeemed in 2022, to $83,000 redeemed in 2023, and $122,000 redeemed in 2024; and


    WHEREAS, in 2025 BFBL-GLV and Two Rivers Health and Wellness Foundation ran a pilot program which provided $10 for every $5 Senior FMNP voucher, tripling the value of Senior FMNP benefits; and


    WHEREAS, despite the increase in redemption spurred by benefit increases, over the past decade around $1.3 million in Senior FMNP funds have gone unredeemed; and


    WHEREAS, these unused vouchers represent not only a failure to deliver nutritional support for our seniors but also decreased revenue for our county farmers; and


    WHEREAS, lack of transportation options to participating farmers’ markets is a key reason why vouchers may go unredeemed; and


    WHEREAS, the Lehigh and Northampton Transit Authority (LANTA) operates LANtaVan, a door-to-door shared ride (paratransit) service available to eligible riders, including clients of the Northampton County Area Agency on Aging; and


    WHEREAS, the average weekday paratransit ridership exceeded 1,000 trips per day prior to the COVID-19 pandemic but is now at only around 800 passenger trips a day.



    NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Northampton County Council encourages the Northampton County Area Agency on Aging to pursue a pilot program with LANTA to utilize paratransit vans to shuttle individuals from Northampton County Senior Centers to producer-only farmers’ markets and back.


    BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Senior FMNP vouchers should be made available to seniors participating in the pilot shuttle program.

 


    As there were no comments or questions, Mr. Kraft called for the vote on the resolution.


    The vote: Boulette, “yes”; Keegan, “yes”; Kraft, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Giovanni, “yes” and Holland, “yes.”


    The resolution was adopted by a vote of 9-0.



    Mr. Warren made a motion to amend the agenda to add a resolution regarding the Administrative Code Article XIII contract with Wilmer R. Schultz, Inc., for the replacement of the parking deck. He added that the contract itself had previously been approved by Council, and in appreciation for the need to replace the parking deck as soon as possible, he wanted to consider the contract approval without delay.


    Ms. Fadem seconded the motion.


    Mr. Kraft called for the vote on the motion.


    The vote: Warren, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Kraft, “yes”; Qayyum, “no”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Boulette, “yes”; Giovanni, “yes”; Holland, “yes” and Keegan, “yes.”


    The motion to amend the agenda to introduce the resolution passed by a vote of 8-1.



Consideration of Administrative Code Article XIII Contract Resolution: Wilmer R. Schultz, Inc.


    Mr. Boulette introduced the following resolution:


R.81-2026. WHEREAS, Northampton County Administrative Code Article XIII Procurement and Disposition of County Property, Section 13.15 Contracts and Agreements c.(1) requires approval of County Council for "...any contract exceeding $100,000, which was awarded using the Competitive Negotiation, Negotiation After Competitive Sealed Bidding and Non‑Competitive Negotiation source selection methods. For contracts with renewal clauses, the entire potential payout if all renewal clauses are exercised under the terms of the contract must be considered when determining if Council approval is necessary;” and

 

WHEREAS, on July 31, 2026, the Northampton County Council received a request from the County Executive for County Council to adopt a resolution endorsing a contract with Wilmer R. Schultz, Inc., to serve as the Government Center Parking Deck Replacement Project – General Contractor Prime Contract, for a term of two (2) years, at a total cost of $11,605,000.

NOW, THEREFORE IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED that the Northampton County Council does hereby concur with the recommendation of the County Executive, as set forth in the attached documentation, to approve the contract with Wilmer R. Schultz, Inc.  

IT IS FURTHER RESOLVED, with the adoption of this Resolution, Resolution No. 51-2026, is hereby rescinded. 

Mr. Kraft indicated that they had previously reviewed the specifications of the contract and prior bids.

    As there were no further comments or questions, Mr. Kraft called for the vote on the resolution.


    The vote: Boulette, “yes”; Qayyum, “yes”; Vargo Heffner, “yes”; Warren, “yes”; Fadem, “yes”; Giovanni, “yes”; Holland, “yes”; Kraft, “yes” and Keegan, “yes.”


    The resolution was adopted by a vote of 9-0.



    Solicitor Deschler stated that the agenda as amended should be posted online and at the Clerk's office within one business day.



Council Committee Reports


    Mr. Warren advised that the Economic Development Committee had met and discussed the 2026 CDBG grants and also had a presentation from ArtsQuest.


    Mr. Warren stated the Human Services Committee received an update from the Department of Veterans Affairs as well as the Division of Children, Youth and Families.


    Mr. Kraft advised that a pre-bid meeting was held for the updates on the audio/visual to the Council meeting room, and that bids were due back on August 19th with plans to discuss the bids at the September Finance Committee meeting.


             

Council Liaison Report


    Mr. Boulette stated that the Industrial Development Authority met and had reported a clean fiscal year audit, elected new officers, and stated that they had been informed that the Dixie redevelopment project was going to proceed utilizing a TIF from just the Borough of Wilson and Wilson Area School District. He further stated they had to get a new site study done to ensure that the new tax numbers met all of the tax credit requirements.


    Mr. Qayyum advised he attended the Northampton County Housing Authority meeting, and reported that all County public housing sites were at over 95% occupancy, with 540 vouchers awarded. He further advised that the occupancy rate across all public housing was 90.74%.


     Mr. Qayyum stated the Airport Authority had moved their meeting to the following month.



    Mr. Qayyum advised that he felt they owed it to the public and future Councils to carefully examine what they were trying to do with the Employee Policy Manual (EPM). He gave a background of the issue between prior Councils and prior Executives, including the litigation in 2008, and advised that in spite of the history, Executives were still using the exception clause in the Career Services Regulations (CSR), without approval from Council. He advised that in 2015, Council led by Mr. Lamont McClure refused to concede the power of determining salary, and determined that County Executive John Brown’s attempt to unilaterally grant raises in 2015 was a clear violation of the Home Rule Charter and the Administrative Code.


    Mr. Qayyum stated that Council was now proposing a codified Executive authority to grant step increases for employees up to Step 3 that he could not support. He further stated that this practice was using an exception clause that was never codified or approved by County Council, and the EPM had never come to Council or the Personnel Commission. He stated that Council clearly had the power to set salaries, and if the Executive wanted to grant step increases to exempt employees, they could justify that to Council. He further stated that was not restricting authority, but instead was enforcing the Charter. He went on to say that the 2015 Council was not fighting over Career Service classifications, but were instead defending the principle that the Executive could not unilaterally approve raises without Council oversight.


    Mr. Kraft advised that the situation was different than 2015, where the Executive was giving out raises to people without approval. He further advised what happened this year was the County Executive asked to appoint a qualified person to a Cabinet position, and asked for County Council to approve the step level that she thought was appropriate for that individual.



    Mr. Warren stated that he attended the annual conference of the County Commissioners Association of Pennsylvania (CCAP), and that he sat on the Technology Committee. He further stated that there was a discussion with a lot of sobering ideas with regard to artificial intelligence (AI) and its effects on counties in the future. He stated that in Berks County, they had 300,000 AI based right to know requests, and Northampton had to be prepared to deal with a similar situation.


    Ms. Vargo Heffner advised that at CCAP, she attended the Human Services and Courts and Corrections Committee meetings, and stated they had started a Health Task Force Advisory Group to review the State health crisis that developed through increasing health deserts with no services. She further advised that legislation considering body cameras for probation officers was now in the PA Senate, and this was merely the right to have body cameras, rather than a mandatory requirement.


    Mr. Boulette stated that he had attended the CCAP Governance Committee meeting, where they discussed a new law that would require Chief Assessment Officers for each county to maintain contact information for property owners any time a property was sold or anytime a municipality in the county issued a code violation. In response to a question from Mr. Kraft, Mr. Boulette  stated this would allow for the tracking of landlords who had a history of violations.


    Mr. Boulette advised that the CCAP Economic Development Committee meeting informed attendees that the tax credit program known as the Neighborhood Partnership Program, which the state used to support community revitalization efforts through grants, was being discontinued. He further advised that if there were areas with multicultural plans being benefited under this program, they should put something out to the State Department of Economic Development to encourage them to continue this program. He stated Slate Belt Rising currently benefited from this program.



    In response to questions from Mr. Qayyum, Mr. Kraft stated that as President of Council he had the opportunity to select 5 voting attendees to the CCAP meeting. He further stated that he felt the County Executive should have a vote, but he felt that CCAP existed primarily as a lobbying body. Mr. Qayyum stated that a Council Member who was running for a CCAP position did not receive a vote, and Mr. Kraft said he was not aware of anyone running for  a CCAP office, and the selection of who voted was a prerogative of the President.

                            

    Mr. Giovanni advised that he had also attended CCAP, and attended a meeting where reassessment was discussed. He further advised that assessment requirements could be coming in the near future, and stated that counties needed to consider how to deal with data centers and how they affected our environment and our electric bills.



Adjournment


    Ms. Keegan made a motion to adjourn the meeting.


    Mr. Giovanni seconded the motion.


    The motion to adjourn passed unanimously by acclamation.




                           ______________________________

                                   Alene M. Shafnisky

                                   Clerk to Council

1.     Public Hearing of an Ordinance Entitled, “AN ORDINANCE OF THE COUNCIL OF THE COUNTY OF NORTHAMPTON, NORTHAMPTON COUNTY, PENNSYLVANIA, AUTHORIZING THE INCURRING OF NONELECTORAL DEBT BY THE ISSUANCE OF GENERAL OBLIGATION BONDS IN AN AGGREGATE PRINCIPAL AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED SIXTY-THREE MILLION FIVE HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS ($63,500,000.00); COVENANTING TO PAY, AND PLEDGING ALL AVAILABLE TAXING POWER OF THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT FOR THE PAYMENT OF THE BONDS; PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A SINKING FUND AND APPOINTING A SINKING FUND DEPOSITORY; FIXING THE FORM, MAXIMUM INTEREST RATES, MATURITY DATES AND OTHER PROVISIONS FOR THE PAYMENT THEREOF; AUTHORIZING THE ACCEPTANCE OF A PROPOSAL FOR THE PURCHASE OF THE BONDS; AUTHORIZING A FILING OF REQUIRED DOCUMENTS WITH THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNITY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT; RATIFYING AND DIRECTING CERTAIN ACTIONS OF OFFICERS; AND MAKING CERTAIN OTHER COVENANTS AND PROVISIONS IN RESPECT OF THE BONDS”


2.     Public Hearing of an Ordinance Entitled, “AN ORDINANCE PROVIDING FOR THE FORMAL ISSUANCE OF PRINTED AND BOUND BUDGETARY INFORMATION NECESSARY FOR THE LEGITIMATE AND PRESCRIBED FINANCIAL OVERSIGHT RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE NORTHAMPTON COUNTY COUNCIL”



New Business



1.     Introduction of an Ordinance Entitled, “AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE 2024 NORTHAMPTON COUNTY BUDGET: COUNTY WIDE – SALARIES AND FRINGES; DEPARTMENT OF FISCAL AFFAIRS – BALANCING OF THE BUDGET; DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNITY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT – COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT GRANTS; DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATION – EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT, ELECTIONS GRANT; PUBLIC DEFENDER’S OFFICE; DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS; DEPARTMENT OF HUMAN SERVICES – ADMINISTRATION, HOMELESS ASSISTANCE, DEVELOPMENT FUND, GRANTS, CHILDREN YOUTH AND FAMILIES, AREA AGENCY ON AGING, HEALTHCHOICES, MENTAL HEALTH, DEVELOPMENTAL PROGRAMS, EARLY INTERVENTION, DRUG AND ALCOHOL, OPIOID FUNDS”


2.  Consideration of a Northampton County Ban on Open Burning Resolution
